content: The studies reviewed provide detailed insights into the effects of physical activity on various health outcomes in populations with specific conditions, such as Parkinson’s disease, stroke, major depression, and schizophrenia. 1. Dance Interventions in Parkinson’s Disease: A systematic review by Dos Santos Delabary (2018) included five randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with 159 participants, primarily older men aged 61 to 72 years, across all stages of Parkinson’s disease (Hoehn & Yahr stages 0–4). Dance interventions, predominantly tango classes, were conducted for at least three weeks. Participants in the dance groups demonstrated improvements in motor symptoms (measured by the Unified Parkinson’s Disease Rating Scale Part III), functional mobility (Timed Up and Go test), endurance (6-Minute Walk Test), freezing of gait (FOG-Q), and walking velocity (both forward and backward) compared to no intervention or other forms of exercise. However, most differences were not statistically significant. The evidence was rated as moderate, with serious concerns about indirectness and imprecision. 2. Nordic Walking in Parkinson’s Disease: Cugusi (2017) reviewed six RCTs with 221 participants aged 40 to 80 years, with a disease duration of 5 to 7 years (Hoehn & Yahr stages 1–4). Interventions compared Nordic walking to other exercise protocols or no exercise over 4 to 24 weeks. Results were mixed. Some studies showed superior outcomes for Nordic walking in measures such as the 6-Minute Walk Test and Timed Up and Go test, while others favored alternative exercise protocols. The evidence was rated as moderate, with concerns about inconsistency and indirectness. 3. Aerobic, Resistance, and Coordination Exercises in Parkinson’s Disease: Stuckenschneider (2019) analyzed 11 RCTs with 508 participants (mean age 68 years, Hoehn & Yahr stages 1–4). Interventions included aerobic, resistance, and coordination exercises lasting 4 to 26 weeks. Evidence on cognitive outcomes was mixed. Only one study reported a statistically significant improvement in global cognitive function, while three studies found effects on executive function. No significant effects were observed for memory, attention, or processing speed. The evidence was rated as moderate, with serious concerns about indirectness. 4. Physical Activity in Stroke Survivors: Bonini-Rocha (2018) reviewed 11 RCTs with 750 participants aged 38 to 91 years, 1 to 157 months post-stroke. Circuit-based exercises were conducted 2 to 7 times per week for 30 to 90 minutes per session over 4 to 19 weeks. Improvements were observed in walking function, but no significant effects were found for balance or functional mobility. The evidence was rated as moderate, with serious concerns about bias, indirectness, and imprecision. 5. Tai Chi and Traditional Chinese Exercises in Stroke Survivors: Li (2018) reviewed five RCTs with 346 participants aged 55 to 73 years. Tai Chi interventions lasting 6 to 12 weeks were evaluated for their effects on standing balance and gait ability. Significant improvements were observed in balance and gait among Tai Chi participants compared to controls. The evidence was rated as low due to serious concerns about bias and indirectness. 6. Pilates in Stroke Survivors: Miranda (2018) included two RCTs with 39 participants aged 63 to 68 years. Pilates interventions were compared to control groups. One study reported greater improvements in functional status (Timed Up and Go test) and cardiorespiratory fitness (VO2 max) in the Pilates group, while the other found better balance outcomes. The evidence was rated as moderate, with concerns about indirectness. 7. High-Intensity Interval Training (HIIT) in Stroke Survivors: Wiener (2019) reviewed three RCTs and three before-after studies with 140 participants. HIIT protocols involved treadmill or bicycle training for 20 to 30 minutes per session, 2 to 5 times per week, over 2 to 8 weeks. Significant improvements in cardiorespiratory fitness were observed, but these were not statistically different from moderate-intensity exercise groups. No consistent effects were found for balance or functional mobility. The evidence was rated as low due to serious concerns about indirectness and imprecision. 8. Physical Activity in Major Depression: Krogh (2017) reviewed nine RCTs with 827 participants aged 21 to 75 years. Interventions included various exercise intensities and types compared to control groups. No statistically significant differences in quality of life (QOL) scores were observed between exercise and control groups. The evidence was rated as very low due to serious concerns about bias, inconsistency, and indirectness. 9. Physical Activity in Schizophrenia: Limited evidence suggests that physical activity may improve health-related outcomes in individuals with schizophrenia. However, the certainty of evidence is low due to methodological limitations and lack of long-term data. 10. General Observations: Across conditions, moderate-to-vigorous physical activity appears to have beneficial effects on physical and cognitive functions, though the magnitude and consistency of these effects vary. Serious concerns about bias, indirectness, and imprecision frequently limit the strength of conclusions. These findings underscore the potential of tailored physical activity interventions to improve health outcomes in specific populations, while highlighting the need for more rigorous and consistent research methodologies.
